extracted.intended_audience: readers of Popular Science Monthly: educated lay public and scientists interested in medicine, physiology, germ theory, and scientific skepticism
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial/expository guidance on how to evaluate extraordinary scientific claims (e.g., clairvoyance) and on experimental/clinical evidence (germ-theory air tests, chloroform anaesthesia). Emphasizes what kinds of tests and results count as convincing and what practical consequences a genuine discovery should produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific-discovery criterion: new procurable effects
rubrics_metrics.description: All scientific discoveries, in fact, are new procurable effects, and are, therefore, their own witnesses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genuine discovery should deliver new, observable, and repeatable effects (practical consequences or novel facts) that attest to its reality. Mere testimonial or retrospective agreement with known facts is insufficient; the discovery must enable new knowledge or applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectation that extraordinary claims yield novel results
rubrics_metrics.description: Clairvoyance must give us the new results of a marvelously-sharpened vision; the extra faculty implies extra disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claimed extraordinary faculty (e.g., clairvoyance) were real and long demonstrated, it ought to have produced discoveries or applications beyond existing knowledge (e.g., revealing inner constitution of things, new physiological knowledge). Absence of such fruits counts strongly against the claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conclusive behavioural test for clairvoyance (closed-eyes card-reading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Clairvoyance was claimed to be proved by one of the patients repeatedly reading and naming cards while four of the commissioners successively held his eyes closed with their fingers — a test the commissioners called 'absolute conclusiveness.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A convincing demonstration of clairvoyance should use strict controls that preclude ordinary sensory access (e.g., eyes physically closed and held) and be repeatable under independent observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical diagnostic verification (post-mortem confirmation)
rubrics_metrics.description: One of the somnambulists determined correctly the symptoms of M. Marc, and also the disease of another person, the accuracy of the diagnosis being confirmed by post-mortem examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagnostic claims (e.g., of seeing internal disease) should be validated by independent clinical or pathological confirmation (post-mortem exam, laboratory tests) to be accepted as evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand for immediate, demonstrable results from a purported new method
rubrics_metrics.description: All scientific discoveries are new procurable effects...we demand at once the effects that flow immediately from the quality of the discovery; in fact, we only know it by these results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a purported method or faculty, require that it produce outcomes that are immediately detectable or utilizable; absence of immediate demonstrable effects undermines the claim's credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Air-sterilization / germ-sampling experimental method
rubrics_metrics.description: Tyndall's experiment: sterilize a bottle of infusion, open it upon the brink of a precipice (high elevation), after contact with the air recork it and observe whether the infusion retained its sterility; Pasteur bottled air at high Paris points, Mont Blanc, and streets to compare putrefactive power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rigorous tests of airborne germ presence require sterilized controls, standardized sampling at distinct locations (street-level vs high elevation), and direct comparison of putrefactive/fermentative outcomes. Such controlled comparative sampling is presented as decisive evidence for variation in germ load with elevation and local conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical correlation criterion for airborne germs (environmental distribution)
rubrics_metrics.description: Noxious effluvia and organic germ-dust specially hover over low marshes and putrefying cesspools, while the ascent of a mountain of considerable elevation carries us above malaria and aerial infection; air of street levels more laden with microzymes than high points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observational correlations (geography, elevation, proximity to filth) that consistently associate higher rates of putrefaction/disease with certain environments are treated as supporting evidence for germ-based explanations of decay and zymotic disease.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical diagnostic inference: sensibility indicates central nervous system involvement
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever the mind is affected, there appear at the same time symptoms of disordered sensibility, and vice versa. When a patient exhibits notable disorder of the sensibility, then, if the nerves are intact, we can safely conclude that the central nervous system is affected, and to that degree that the mind has not escaped.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In clinical/pathological reasoning, a disorder of sensibility (assuming peripheral nerves are intact) is diagnostic of central nervous system/mind involvement; practitioners should use this inference when assessing mental/neurological disturbance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stages and signs of chloroform intoxication / anaesthesia depth
rubrics_metrics.description: Sequence: initial dizziness, vertigo, dimness of vision, exalted and disordered ideas resembling drunkenness; loss of judgement and active memory; dreaming/somnolence; eventual insensibility (sleep) and then coma with deep sleep, regular respiration, slow full pulse, motionless pupils, and paralyzed features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate depth of anaesthesia by observable behavioural and physiological markers in sequence (mental excitation → disordered ideation → memory loss → insensibility → coma). Memory loss may precede insensibility; once in deep coma the patient will not be aroused by violent external stimuli.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anesthesia administration guideline: account for patient temperament and risk of syncope
rubrics_metrics.description: In administering chloroform, we must take account of the patient's temperament. If he is resolute, all will go on well and the insensibility will readily disappear; if he has an unconquerable dread of the operation, great watchfulness will be necessary, for in such cases syncope is very frequent. Such a patient resists the action of the drug and it must be administered in far greater quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When producing anaesthesia, clinicians should adjust vigilance and dosing to patient temperament; anxious patients may resist/to some degree 'brace' against the drug, show delayed insensibility, or be more liable to syncope — requiring increased monitoring and dose adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical relevance of pain without memory under anaesthesia
rubrics_metrics.description: If an acute penetrating pain continues only a short time but all memory of it disappeared at once, then the patient would deny that he had suffered at all and would not hesitate to undergo the operation again — in short, he would have enjoyed the benefits of chloroformic anaesthesia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of anaesthetic adequacy may consider whether painful events are retained in memory; absence of recall can meaningfully reduce the clinical/ethical impact of brief intraoperative pain, though observable distress at the time still occurs.
